markdown:
The station's bridge plunged into a muted blue twilight—the observation mode for rare phenomena. On the central screen, fed by a network of orbital relays, a black blotch crawled: the Moon was obscuring the Sun over Mexico, and along the thin strip of the total phase, millions of tiny dots flowed—people who had come to stand in the shadow.

Kluk stood by the hull; the nap of his soft shell trembled slightly. He could feel them. Millions of heartbeats, tightened in anticipation. The dampness of palms. Tears that people did not hold back as they gazed at the black disk within the corona. It was a heavy, warm sensation, as if the entire station had suddenly filled with thick honey.

"Saros one hundred thirty-nine," Querr turned his crystalline body toward the projection, his facets casting multicolored splashes of graphs onto the panels. "The cycle repeats approximately every eighteen years and eleven days. The next total eclipse in the continental United States—August twenty-third, twenty forty-four. Umbra. Maximum phase: four minutes and twenty-eight seconds."

He froze, seemingly awaiting an acknowledgment of the logic of intellectual superiority, but only the hum of the ventilation hung in the bridge.

"I am serious," Querr clicked his resonator, and a dry list floated onto the screen: fuel, kilocalories, man-hours, metric tons of carbon emitted into the atmosphere. "Why migrate across a continent for an astronomical show that will return in eighteen years?"

"It's not about the shadow," Kluk said softly. His soft paws curled into little balls. "It's about the fact that the shadow leaves."

"A banal euphemism for the rotation of solid bodies," Querr replied.

"They are crying," Kluk insisted. "They are hugging. They know that this will not happen again."

"For them," Querr corrected. "Finitude is a bug of their biology, not a feature of the event. In eighteen years, they will see the same thing, just at a different point on the planet."

Kluk, curled in a ring by the console, suddenly changed color from indigo to orange—the color of urgent interest. Strange cardboard glasses with blacked-out lenses were already perched on his optical stalks, and he was attempting to put another pair over the first.

"I have eight pairs!" he announced joyfully. His voice sounded muffled due to the multilayered cardboard. "Eleven, if you count the spare ones with glitter. Who wants to try on a cultural code?"

"I am searching for signs of aggressive mobilization," Brax grumbled, running a scanner over the crowds of people on the screen. "Look: population density is increasing seventeenfold. Everyone is looking at one point. This is the perfect cover for..."

"For what? For a collective 'wow'?" Querr turned to Plush. "You are attempting to translate emotional noise into arguments. This is incorrect. Statistics are relentless: the event is cyclical."

"Statistics don't feel," Kluk said, stepping closer. "For a human standing there, on Earth, this might be the only total phase of their life. The path is narrow, they have to reach it, and a human life is short. This is... the last shadow they will see."

"An artificial limitation of perspective," Querr concluded ruthlessly.

Inside the suit of the Nine, nine voices suddenly buzzed simultaneously:

"I propose darkening the bridge for clarity!"

"Eighteen percent efficiency, Red, don't waste energy!"

"Blue supports the darkening!"

"Green is against it, we are losing visual contact!"

"Yellow abstains and is brewing tea!"

"...Four for, four against, one tea," the Voice of the Nine summarized, and the bridge jerked. The lighting flickered, went out for half a second, and came back on, but now with the greenish tint of an old fluorescent lamp.

"Your collective intelligence," OKO's voice spoke insinuatingly from the walls, blending Victorian politeness with nineties internet slang, "demonstrates a striking inability to interpret primates. I envy your simplicity."

Kluk froze. He looked at the screen, where the shadow already half-covered the Sun, and felt the earthly excitement reaching critical mass—the tremor before the inevitable departure. He realized that words were powerless. But he knew how to show them.

"Then we will experience this together with them," Kluk said.

He approached the environment control panel. His soft fingers, designed for the gentle handling of fragile human emotions, moved with surgical precision—he activated the direct broadcast protocol.

"Regulation violation," OKO announced immediately. "Data archiving is mandatory for all observation sessions."

"Turn off the recording," Plush asked. "Turn off the replays, turn off the archiving. For four minutes and twenty-eight seconds. We will watch the live broadcast as a unique moment. Like they do."

"Data loss," Querr objected. His crystalline facets flashed an alarming yellow. "Irreversible degradation of scientific material."

"This isn't science," Plush said. "This is a shadow that leaves."

"Vote!" the Nine commanded.

"For viewing without recording!" Red shouted.

"Against data loss!" Green countered.

"Does anyone see what's happening?" Kluk complained, trying to remove the third pair of glasses without removing the second. "Everything is black for me!"

"Security does not object to a temporary suspension of archiving," Brax said unexpectedly, putting away his scanner. "If... if it is necessary for understanding the threat."

"Four for," the Voice of the Nine summarized. "Four against. One..."

"Yellow believes the tea will get cold if we don't decide," the final voice intervened.

"No decision reached," OKO sighed. "A gap in the scientific archive requires the consent of the keeper."

Querr looked at the dry graphs once more, then cleared them from the screen with a gesture.

"Four minutes and twenty-eight seconds," he pronounced. "I permit it."

"The decision is now reached. Direct broadcast protocol activated. Recording disabled. Replays unavailable. You are living in the present. How primitive," OKO announced.

The screen went dark for a fraction of a second, and when it returned, the total phase was already there—the black disk of the Moon, the silvery corona, and the shadows of people on Earth, merged into one trembling whole. Silence fell over the bridge.

"I'll turn on the camera in the frame!" Kluk shrieked, clicking the temples of his "eclipse" glasses and trying to activate a hidden module. "This isn't an archive, it's... personal insurance!"

"Any copying violates the direct broadcast protocol," OKO replied coldly, and Kluk's lenses instantly darkened, blocked by the system. "Your eyes are now for original viewing only. Like the primates."

"Then at least the security archive!" Brax barked, raising his scanner. "There must be a trace left for the investigation!"

"The trace will remain in your bio-memory," OKO sighed. "Or in your nightmares. Depending on your susceptibility."

A hurried vote stirred within the suit of the Nine:

"Personal sketches are permissible! Four for!"

"Protocol violation! Four against!"

"One suggests finishing the tea first!"

"Abstention accepted," OKO stated. "Four for, four against, one tea. A tie. No sketches. Only immediate experience. What a pity."

And silence followed. Not the kind that occurs during an accident, but the kind born when a moment hangs in the air without a network, without a backup copy, without the possibility to rewind. Kluk looked at the screen, where the black disk hung in a silvery halo, and felt the earthly tremor fill the bridge—an unspoken understanding that this is now, and only now.

He looked at Querr. The archivist's crystalline facets, which usually flickered rapidly with reflections of data and calculations, suddenly slowed. They stopped racing through numbers and graphs and froze, holding only one image—the black circle of the eclipse floating in the darkness. Querr stood motionless, and something changed in his transparent structure—not the color, not the shape, but some internal quality of movement, as if his entire infinite archive had fallen silent for a moment, giving way to the stillness.

"This..." Querr's voice sounded different: quieter, drier, without its former skepticism. "Statistics do not convey... the shiver."

Kluk did not answer. He saw how Querr's crystals slowly, almost imperceptibly, leaned toward the screen—not because there was data there, but because there was something there that could not be saved.

The four minutes and twenty-eight seconds ended. Light returned to the screen, the solar disk began to emerge from behind the Moon, and OKO announced in the standard voice of a concierge:

"Broadcast complete. Archiving resumed. You have experienced an irreversible moment. Congratulations."

The crew exhaled. Kluk slowly returned to indigo; Brax cautiously lowered his scanner. Querr turned to Plush, and in his usually brilliant facets, something new could be read—almost shyness.

"Perhaps," the archivist said dryly, "in the 'bug of finitude'... there is its own aesthetic logic. Data loss... is sometimes justified."

Kluk looked at his colleagues—beings who had lived through more human civilizations than there were to count. He realized that even they, with their extraordinarily long lives, needed to be reminded sometimes of the value of a moment. Otherwise, they risked turning into soulless archives, storing everything but feeling nothing.

"I require carbohydrate compensation for stress," Brax announced.

"Vote!" the Nine commanded.

"Pizza!" all nine voices inside the suit shouted in unison. "Unanimous! Nine for! Zero against! Zero abstentions!"

Tarra stood in the shadow of the entrance, observing from the side. Her anthropologist's jacket with piping was draped over her shoulders. Plush saw her take out an old paper notebook—worn, with a peeling spine—quickly write something, and then close it without sending the data to the network. She looked at the screen, where the eclipse shadow was already crawling toward the ocean, and lightly, almost imperceptibly, pushed aside the holo-tablet with the Report on Humanity's Readiness for First Contact.

"Oops," Kluk suddenly said, removing the stack of cardboard glasses from his optical stalks. "I didn't see anything. I had eight pairs on my eyes, and still, I didn't see anything!"

"Recording is absent," OKO reminded him coldly. "You made a collective decision for a direct broadcast. Playback is impossible."

"But... but how will I know what was there?" Kluk froze, looking at the glasses in his paws. "And why do they smell like tea?"

"That's Yellow," the Nine sighed.

Kluk watched as Kluk took off the eclipse glasses. The ones he had pulled from the archive three hours ago, boasting of a rare earthly artifact, now looked like nothing more than two dark circles of plastic in his pliable fingers. On the console before them, the recording indicator glowed as a blank green zero—not a single petabyte, not a single replay. Beyond the viewport, the Moon's shadow was receding from the edge of the solar disk, and rectangles of light returned to the fields where people were already closing their trunks. Kluk felt a strange warmth beneath his soft nap—not from the climate control, but from the fact that this specific moment, when Kluk held human glasses in his hands and breathed together with the planet, now existed only in their memory. Nowhere else.
title: Scheduled Eclipse
